lesson.architecture.title: CPU architecture (amd64 vs. arm64)
lesson.architecture.desc: Why a template must match the host CPU.
lesson.architecture.why.title: What is this about?
lesson.architecture.why.body:
Every CPU family has its own instruction set. A program is compiled for exactly one instruction set. If it runs on a different architecture you get: `Exec format error`.

**amd64** (also x86_64, x64): Intel/AMD PCs, laptops, most servers.
**arm64** (also aarch64): Apple Silicon Macs, Raspberry Pi 4/5, smartphones.

LXC and Docker containers share the kernel and CPU of the host. The template must have the same architecture as the host. VMs can only run a foreign architecture through emulation (QEMU), which is very slow.

Your host reports via the API: **{hostArch}**.
lesson.architecture.host.title: Check the host architecture
lesson.architecture.host.body: Open **Node → Shell** and run the commands. `uname -m` shows x86_64 or aarch64, `dpkg --print-architecture` shows amd64 or arm64, `file /bin/ls` shows which architecture a program was built for.
lesson.architecture.ctarch.title: Container architecture
lesson.architecture.ctarch.body: Checks via the API whether the architecture of the selected container ({vmid}) matches the host ({hostArch}).
lesson.architecture.templates.title: Templates in the `local` storage
lesson.architecture.templates.body: Checks via the API whether the `local` storage contains templates of a foreign architecture (name contains {foreignArch}). Such templates cause `Exec format error` on this host.
lesson.architecture.download.title: Download the right template
lesson.architecture.download.body: Replace `<version>` with the version from the list. You remove the wrong template with `pveam remove`. This cannot be undone, so check the name first.
lesson.architecture.rule.title: Rule of thumb
lesson.architecture.rule.body:
**For every download (ISO, template, Docker image, binary), check the architecture in the file name.**

Extra trap: building Docker images on an Apple Silicon Mac. There you need `docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64 ...`.

From practice: an arm64 template on an amd64 host only showed `termproxy` / “Failed to spawn”. Only `pct start --debug` named the cause (lesson 4).
lesson.snapshot.title: Snapshot & rollback
lesson.snapshot.desc: Freeze a state and go back when something breaks.
lesson.snapshot.intro.title: What is this about?
lesson.snapshot.intro.body:
A snapshot freezes the state of a container. Before any risky change (update, configuration) you take a snapshot and can go back if something goes wrong.

The name starts with a letter, with no spaces and no umlauts.
lesson.snapshot.state.title: 1. Create a state
lesson.snapshot.state.body: Run the command **inside the container** (not on the host).
lesson.snapshot.take.title: 2. Take a snapshot
lesson.snapshot.take.body: In the interface: **CT → Snapshots → Take Snapshot**, name e.g. `vor_test`. Or run the command on the host. The check reports as soon as there is a snapshot other than `current`.
lesson.snapshot.break.title: 3. Break something
lesson.snapshot.break.body: Again **inside the container**: delete the test file.
lesson.snapshot.rollback.title: 4. Rollback
lesson.snapshot.rollback.body: **Snapshots → select `{snap}` → Rollback**. The container stops briefly; start it again afterwards if needed. Careful: changes made after the snapshot are lost. The check looks for a successful rollback task since this step began.
lesson.snapshot.verify.title: 5. Verify
lesson.snapshot.verify.body: Again **inside the container**: the file is back if the rollback worked.
lesson.snapshot.rule.title: Rule of thumb
lesson.snapshot.rule.body: **Snapshot ≠ backup.** A snapshot lives on the same disk. If the disk dies, the snapshot is gone too.
lesson.backup.title: Backup & restore
lesson.backup.desc: Create an independent backup and test the restore.
lesson.backup.intro.title: What is this about?
lesson.backup.intro.body:
A backup (vzdump) is an independent file that you can store on other storage and use to recreate the container.

**Snapshot:** same disk, quick way back before a change, rule: before changes.
**Backup:** its own file, ideally on other storage, survives a disk failure, rule: regular and scheduled.
lesson.backup.now.title: 1. Create a backup
lesson.backup.now.body: **CT → Backup → Backup now**: storage `local`, mode `Snapshot` (the container keeps running), compression `ZSTD`. Or use the command on the host. The check looks for a new backup of CT {vmid}.
lesson.backup.job.title: 2. Scheduled backup
lesson.backup.job.body: **Datacenter → Backup → Add**: time e.g. 03:00, select the container, retention **Keep Last: 3**. The check only verifies that at least one job exists, not its settings.
lesson.backup.restore.title: 3. Test the restore
lesson.backup.restore.body: The most important step. In the interface: **local → Backups → Restore** with a new CT ID. Or use the command. `--unique` assigns a new MAC address so there is no network conflict with the original. The new ID is {newid}; the check looks for that container.
lesson.backup.test.title: 4. Check the restored container
lesson.backup.test.body: Start the new container, check that everything is there, and delete it afterwards.
lesson.backup.rule.title: Rules of thumb
lesson.backup.rule.body:
**A backup whose restore was never tested is not a backup.**

Backups on the same disk are only an exercise. Real protection needs other storage (external disk, NAS, Proxmox Backup Server).
lesson.debug.title: Container will not start: debugging
lesson.debug.desc: Find the cause with pct start --debug.
lesson.debug.story.title: The problem
lesson.debug.story.body: In the web interface the console does not open (`termproxy` error) and starting the CT reports “Failed to spawn”. The error message is too generic. Only the debug start shows the cause.
lesson.debug.debug.title: 1. Debug start
lesson.debug.debug.body: Run it on the host (**Node → Shell**). The output appears in the terminal; the extension does not read it.
lesson.debug.cause.title: 2. Read the cause
lesson.debug.cause.body:
**The actual cause is usually at the very bottom.**

Typical causes:
• `Exec format error` → wrong architecture (lesson 1)
• Missing features for Docker in LXC → `nesting=1,keyctl=1`
lesson.debug.config.title: 3. Look at the configuration
lesson.debug.config.body: Shows the configuration of the container.
lesson.debug.running.title: Is the container running?
lesson.debug.running.body: Checks via the API whether CT {vmid} has the status `running`.
lesson.debug.errors.title: No new errors
lesson.debug.errors.body: Checks that no new failed task for CT {vmid} appeared since this step began.
lesson.debug.rule.title: Rule of thumb
lesson.debug.rule.body: **Do not guess, read the debug output.** The first guess (Proxmox version does not fit Debian 13) was wrong. The debug output showed the real cause in a single line.
lesson.permissions.title: Users, realms & permissions
lesson.permissions.desc: Who signs in and what they may do: realm, role, path.
lesson.permissions.realms.title: Realms: where does the password come from?
lesson.permissions.realms.body:
Proxmox separates **who** signs in (user + realm) from **what** they may do (role on a path). This lets you restrict exercises to a single test CT.

`pam`: Linux users of the host. The password comes from Linux (`passwd`), the user must exist on the system.
`pve`: Proxmox-own users ("Proxmox VE authentication server"). The password is set in Proxmox (`pveum passwd`).

The user name always includes the realm: `lab@pve` and `lab@pam` are **two different users**.
lesson.permissions.user.title: 1. Create the user
lesson.permissions.user.body: Run on the host as `root@pam`. First look at what exists with `pveum user list`. If you create the user in a different realm than the one used for the password, you get "does not exist (500)". Sign-in in the web UI: user name `lab`, realm **Proxmox VE authentication server**.
lesson.permissions.roles.title: 2. Assign roles
lesson.permissions.roles.body: Each line assigns a role on a path. `/` applies everywhere (PVEAuditor: read only), `/vms/{vmid}` only to the test CT {vmid}, `/storage/local` for backups on `local`. Permissions are inherited downwards, more specific paths add to them. The last command shows the effective permissions.
lesson.permissions.audit.title: 3. Check read access everywhere
lesson.permissions.audit.body: Checks via the API whether the signed-in user has `Sys.Audit` on `/`. Sign in as `lab@pve` to check; as `root@pam` the check always passes.
lesson.permissions.snapshot.title: 4. Check snapshots on the test CT
lesson.permissions.snapshot.body: Checks whether the signed-in user has `VM.Snapshot` on `/vms/{vmid}`.
lesson.permissions.read.title: 5. Check read access
lesson.permissions.read.body: Calls `/nodes/{node}/status`. With the right you get a response, without it error 403 and the panel shows which right is missing.
lesson.permissions.rule.title: Rule of thumb
lesson.permissions.rule.body:
**The realm is part of the name.** `@pam` ≠ `@pve`.
**As few rights as possible, as many as necessary:** read everywhere, write only on the test CT.
**403 means: signed in, but not permitted.** 401 means: not (or no longer) signed in.
What the host shell needs (`pveam`, `pct start --debug`) stays with `root@pam`.
